answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Credited to Rumi almost everywhere it appears, and the image is thoroughly Rumi-like — but no Persian original, no named translator and no work of Rumi’s has ever been produced for it. Its documented trail stops at a 2006 American self-help anthology, more than seven centuries after Rumi died, where it is printed with no source at all.

source.heading: Where the wording actually comes from

source.excerpt: You were born with wings. Why prefer to crawl through life?
trail: The line is not in Wikiquote’s sourced material. Wikiquote’s Rumi page ↗ files it under Attributed, and the only citation it offers is Larry Chang, Wisdom for the Soul: Five Millennia of Prescriptions for Spiritual Healing (2006), p. 26.

Going to that anthology directly closes the loop rather than opening one. The scanned 2006 edition ↗ carries the sentence on p. 26 credited only to “Jalaluddin Rumi, 1207–1273” — no work, no translator, no Persian. A general-interest quotation anthology is the end of the trail, not a source.

Rumi genuinely writes about wings, and it looks nothing like this. In E. H. Whinfield’s 1898 abridged translation of the Masnavi ↗, Book III runs an extended figure in which knowledge has two wings and mere opinion only one, and Book VI gives the couplet “A bird flies with its wings towards its nest, / The wings of a man are his aspiration and aim.” The imagery is his; this phrasing is not found there.

Fake Rumi verses are common enough that specialists publish debunkings of them, and the test for a fake is documented. Ibrahim Gamard’s Three Fake Rumi Verses ↗ (2019) does not discuss this line, but it shows the method: a verse is treated as spurious when it has no equivalent in the earliest Persian manuscripts of Rumi’s Divan, such as Furūzānfar’s ten-volume critical edition.
source.excerptNote: This is how it appears on p. 26 of Chang’s anthology, under the heading Accomplishment / Achievement / Excellence, credited simply “~ Jalaluddin Rumi, 1207–1273 ~”. Chang cites a work where he has one — Hesiod is given Works and Days, Cicero De Finibus Bonorum et Malorum, Bashō The Narrow Road to the Deep North with its translator and year — but for the Rumi line, as for most of the entries on that page (Aristotle, Molière, Longfellow and Frederick Douglass among them), he prints only a name and a pair of dates. The anthology supplies no work for it, and nothing published since has supplied one either.

artifact.linkText: Read the 2006 anthology on the Internet Archive

source.rightsNote: Rumi’s thirteenth-century Persian is long out of copyright, but that says nothing about this English sentence. No work, edition or translator has been identified for it, so there is no first-publication date to reason from — and its earliest documented appearance sits inside a 2006 anthology that is itself in copyright. With the wording’s origin unknown, we assert no rights status rather than assume it is free to reuse.

author.name: Rumi
author.heading: Rumi
author.metaLine: 1207–1273 · Persian poet, Islamic scholar & Sufi mystic
author.bio: Jalāl al-Dīn Muḥammad Rūmī (30 September 1207 – 17 December 1273) was a Sufi mystic, poet and Islamic scholar, born in Wakhsh in present-day Tajikistan and buried in Konya, where the Mevlevi Order — the whirling dervishes — grew up around his teaching. His major works are the six-volume Masnavi, the Divan-e Shams-e Tabrizi and the prose Fihi Ma Fihi. He wrote in Persian, which means every English “Rumi quote” is somebody’s translation — and a striking number of the popular ones turn out to be nobody’s translation of anything.

cite.sourceCitation: Larry Chang, comp. and ed., Wisdom for the Soul: Five Millennia of Prescriptions for Spiritual Healing (Washington, DC: Gnosophia Publishers, 2006), 26 — where the line is credited to “Jalaluddin Rumi, 1207–1273” with no work, translator or Persian source named. Wikiquote lists it under “Attributed,” citing the same page. No Persian original has been identified.

misattribution.heading: Why this one keeps getting pinned on Rumi
misattribution.intro: Nobody appears to have invented this line maliciously. It simply entered circulation already wearing Rumi’s name, and the quote economy never asked it for papers. Three things are worth separating:

items.why: Wikiquote ↗ places it under “Attributed” rather than among his sourced verse, and offers a 2006 quotation anthology as its only citation. That is the status of a line nobody has been able to trace — not one anybody has verified.

Rumi wrote in Persian, so a genuine quotation must arrive through some named translator and edition. Not one of the sources located names either. The anthology itself ↗ gives the line only “Jalaluddin Rumi, 1207–1273”, the same bare name-and-dates it prints for most entries on that page — so it settles nothing about where the English came from.

Both routes are documented by Ibrahim Gamard in Three Fake Rumi Verses ↗: Rückert, in his Ghaselen (1819), fabricated Oriental-sounding, Rumi-esque content with no Persian equivalent in order to reproduce the ghazal form in German; Barks’s much-quoted The Essential Rumi (1993) is described there as an interpretive version worked up from Nicholson’s English. Neither produced this sentence — but they explain how a beautiful, sourceless English line acquires Rumi’s name.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest verdict is narrower than either the fan sites or the debunkers would like: this is a line attributed to Rumi, not one traced to him and not one proven against him. Until somebody produces a Persian original, the only citation that survives scrutiny is Larry Chang’s anthology of 2006, p. 26 ↗ — a book of quotations, not a book of Rumi.

context.heading: The most quoted poet nobody can quote
lead: Rumi is routinely described as the best-selling poet in America, and almost none of his readers can check him. He wrote in Persian; what circulates in English is a chain of translations, loose renderings and, in a fair number of cases, sentences with no Persian behind them at all. That gap is where a line like this one lives — too good to interrogate, too vague to falsify, and attached to a name that makes interrogation feel rude.

What makes this particular quote interesting is that the genuine article is close enough to touch. Rumi really does build long passages out of wings and flight, and he really does set flight against grovelling on the ground. He just does it in service of a different argument: in Whinfield’s 1898 Masnavi, the two wings are knowledge and the one wing is opinion, and the bird that finally lifts off is the one that has stopped guessing. That is a harder, stranger thought than “believe in yourself” — which may be exactly why the sourceless version travels further.
detailsBody: The verification test used by Rumi scholars is not a matter of taste. As Ibrahim Gamard sets it out in Three Fake Rumi Verses ↗, a candidate verse is checked against the earliest Persian manuscripts of Rumi’s Divan, with Furūzānfar’s ten-volume critical edition as the standard reference. A verse with no equivalent there is not Rumi’s, however Rumi-ish it sounds. That test has retired several of the most famous “Rumi” lines in English, including “Come, come, whoever you are”, which Gamard reports scholars assign to a quatrain by Abu Sa’id ibn Abi’l-Khayr.

For the same reason, much of what the general reader “knows” about Rumi has needed correcting by specialists. Gamard’s Common Misconceptions About Rumi ↗, drawing throughout on Franklin Lewis’s Rumi: Past and Present, East and West, works through claims as basic as where the family actually lived — Vakhsh rather than Balkh — and whether Rumi ever met the poet ‘Attar. If the biography needs that much repair, the quotations deserve at least as much scepticism.
